en: Peṭakopadesa 6.
The Section on the Compendium of the Meaning of the Suttas:
The teaching of the Blessed Buddhas is comprised in three ways: in the aggregates (khandha), the elements (dhātu), and the sense bases (āyatana).
Therein, the five aggregates are the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness.
The ten bases of form—namely, the eye and forms up to the body and tangibles—this is the aggregate of form.
Therein, the six classes of feeling are the aggregate of feeling—namely, feeling born of eye-contact up to feeling born of mind-contact—this is the aggregate of feeling.

Therein, the six classes of perception constitute the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*): from the perception of forms up to the perception of mental phenomena—these are the six classes of perception;

this is the aggregate of perception. Therein, the six classes of volition constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*): from volition regarding forms up to volition regarding mental phenomena—these are the six classes of volition;

this is the aggregate of formations. Therein, the six classes of consciousness constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*): from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—these are the six classes of consciousness; this is the aggregate of consciousness.
These are the five aggregates.
What is their full comprehension?
That they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self—this is their full comprehension.
In this context, what is the meaning of "aggregate" (*khandha*)?
The meaning of a heap is the meaning of an aggregate; the meaning of a mass is the meaning of an aggregate; the meaning of a collection is the meaning of an aggregate.

Just as there is a heap of grass, a heap of forest, a log of wood, a mass of fire, a mass of water, or a mass of wind—so too, the inclusion of everything within the aggregates is the meaning of an aggregate.
Therein, the eighteen elements are: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element …pe… the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
These are the eighteen elements.
The full understanding of these is that they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self; this is their full understanding.
In this context, what is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*)?
It is said: the meaning of "element" is the meaning of a constituent part.
"A component" means the sensitivity of the eye, the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*).
Thus, among the five elements, the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is the sense of being delimited.
For the eye-element is indeed delimited.
Thus, regarding the five [aggregates], he further says that the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is stated in the sense of an absolute nature (*pakati*).
Just as one might say, "By nature this person is bilious, phlegmatic, windy, or of combined humors," so too the eye-element by nature is one among all the ten faculties...
[and so on] ...the meaning of "element" is the sense of being distinct (*visabhāga*).
In that regard, what are the twelve bases?
There are six internal and six external.
From the eye base up to the mind base is the internal; from the form base up to the mental-object base is the external.
These are the twelve bases.
What is their full understanding?
That they are impermanent, suffering, perception, and non-self—this is their full understanding.
Furthermore, full understanding is twofold: full understanding as knowledge and full understanding as abandonment.
Therein, "full understanding as knowledge" refers to [knowing] "it is impermanent, it is suffering, it is a perception, it is non-self"; this is full understanding as knowledge.
"Full understanding as abandonment," however, is the abandoning of desire and lust; this is full understanding as abandonment.
In this context, what is the meaning of "base" (āyatana)?
It is said: the meaning of "base" is the meaning of "mode" (ākāra).
Just as there is a source of gold and a source of base metal, and just as various cattle emerge from those two respective modes.
Thus, these oxen that are the mind and mental factors rise up from kamma, the defilements, and the phenomena of suffering.
Furthermore, it is said that the meaning of "āyatana" is the meaning of "source of income" (āyadāna).
Just as a king’s income arises from his sources of revenue, so too is the meaning of "āyatana" the meaning of "source of income."
The Four Noble Truths are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Suffering, in brief, consists of the mental state and the practice of unwholesome states; its origin, in brief, is ignorance and craving; its cessation, in brief, is true knowledge and liberation; and the path, in brief, is serenity and insight.
In that regard, what are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment?
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the noble eightfold path—these are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.

Those states which lead to the Nibbāna of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the Paccekabuddhas, and of their disciples, both past, future, and present—that path consists of the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body;
[he develops] right exertion … the basis for psychic power … [and so on].
The faculties … the powers … In this context, what is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya)?

The meaning of "lord" (indattha) is the meaning of faculty (indriyattha); the meaning of sovereignty (ādhipateyyattha) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of clarity (pasādattha) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of action that is not shared with anyone else (asādhāraṇaṃ kassa kiriyattha) is the meaning of faculty.

The meaning of non-yielding (anavapariyattha) is the meaning of power (balattha); the meaning of firmness (thāmattha) is the meaning of power; the meaning of support (upādāyattha) is the meaning of power; the meaning of stabilization (upatthambhanattha) is the meaning of power. In this context, what are the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)?
The enlightenment factor of mindfulness up to the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Therein, what is the eightfold path?
Right view up to right concentration.
Therein, the Eightfold Path consists of the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
Therein, right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the aggregate of virtue;
right mindfulness, right effort, and right concentration constitute the aggregate of concentration.
Right intention and right view constitute the aggregate of wisdom.
Thus are these three trainings.
Thus, in three ways, the ten terms [are explained]... [and so forth].

Therein, the practitioner established in the aggregate of virtue does not grasp unwholesome hatred; he eradicates the underlying tendency to hatred, extracts the thorn of hatred, fully understands painful feeling, and transcends the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu).

Established in the aggregate of concentration, he does not grasp unwholesome greed; he eradicates the underlying tendency to lust, extracts the thorn of greed, fully understands pleasant feeling, and transcends the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu).

Established in the aggregate of wisdom, one does not cling to unwholesome delusion; one eradicates the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*); one extracts the dart of delusion and the dart of views; one fully understands neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; and one transcends the formless element (*arūpadhātu*).

Thus, by means of these three aggregates, one does not cling to the three unwholesome roots, extracts the four darts, fully understands the three feelings, and transcends the triple element (*tedhātuka*).
In this context, what is ignorance?
Regarding "ignorance concerning the four noble truths," it should be explained in detail according to how it was treated in the section on the "hesitation regarding living beings.
Therein, what is consciousness?
The six groups of consciousness, feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—this is name.
In this context, what is form?
It is the designation of the form derived from the four great elements.
Thus, both that aforementioned name and this form together are called "name-and-form."
Therein, "the sixfold base" refers to the six internal bases: from the eye as an internal base up to the mind as an internal base.
"Contact" refers to the six groups of contact: from eye-contact up to mind-contact.
"Feeling" refers to the six groups of feeling.
Craving (*taṇhā*) refers to the six classes of craving.

Grasping (*upādāna*) refers to the four kinds of grasping: grasping at sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), grasping at views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), grasping at rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and grasping at a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
Existence (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence: the realm of sense-pleasures (*kāmabhava*), the realm of form (*rūpabhava*), and the formless realm (*arūpabhava*).
In this context, what is birth (*jāti*)?

That which is the first arising of the aggregates (*khandha*), the first arising of the elements (*dhātu*), the first arising of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the birth, the production, the descent, the manifestation, and the appearance of the aggregates—this is birth.
In this context, what is aging (*jarā*)?
That which is called aging— namely, brokenness, graying of hair, wrinkling of the skin, the discoloration of the four great elements, and their collapse;
that which is the wasting away, the falling away, the decline and dissolution of the life-span, the disintegration of the faculties,
the withering, and the ripening— this is aging.
In this context, what is death?

Death means: in each respective class of beings, the passing away, the vanishing, the death, the completion of time, the dissolution of the bloated body, the cutting off of the life-faculty—this is death.
Thus, both the aforementioned aging and this death together constitute aging-and-death.

In this context, ignorance (*avijjā*), characterized by the non-comprehension of things as they truly are amidst the darkness of gloom, is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
Volitional formations, characterized by the act of forming, are manifested by the accumulation [of kamma] and the projection of renewed existence;
they are the proximate cause for consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
The physical basis has the characteristic of manifesting consciousness; it is the proximate cause for name-and-form.
Name-and-form has the characteristic of depending on many supports; it is the proximate cause for the six sense bases.
The six sense bases have the characteristic of defining the faculties; they are the proximate cause for contact.
Contact has the characteristic of meeting; it is the proximate cause for feeling.
Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; it is the proximate cause for craving.
Craving has the characteristic of clinging; it is the proximate cause for grasping.
Clinging has the characteristic of grasping; it is the proximate cause for existence.
Existence has the characteristic of scattering into various destinies; it is the proximate cause for birth.
Birth has the characteristic of the manifestation of the aggregates; it is the proximate cause for aging.
Aging has the characteristic of bringing about the maturation of the faculties; it is the proximate cause for death.
Death has the characteristic of the exhaustion of the life-span and the obstruction of vitality; it is the proximate cause for suffering.
Suffering has the characteristic of bodily oppression; it is the proximate cause for mental grief.
Grief has the characteristic of squeezing the mind; it is the proximate cause of sorrow.
Sorrow has the characteristic of grieving; it is the proximate cause of lamentation.
Lamentation has the characteristic of uttering words; it is the proximate cause of despair.
Whatever are sufferings, those are distresses.
There are nine terms wherein the entire side of the unwholesome finds its inclusion and convergence.
What are the nine terms?
There are two root defilements, three unwholesome roots, and four perversions.
Among these, the two root defilements are ignorance and craving for existence; the three unwholesome roots are greed, hatred, and delusion;
and the four perversions are as follows:

“To perceive the impermanent as permanent” is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view; “to perceive suffering as pleasure” is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view;
“to perceive what is non-self as self” is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view;
“to perceive the foul as beautiful” is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
Therein, ignorance (avijjā) is non-knowing as it really is regarding the Four Noble Truths; this is ignorance.
Craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is that which is lust, infatuation, desire, delusion, longing, delight, attachment, and non-renunciation toward states of existence; this is craving for existence.
Therein, what is the unwholesome root of greed (lobha)?

Greed (*lobha*) means: greed, greediness, longing, infatuation, aspiration, delight, cleaving, and non-relinquishing with respect to various others' objects, others' goods, others' places, others' wealth, and others' possessions. This is greed, the unwholesome root.
What is its root?
Greed is the root of unwholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action arising from greed, as it is the root of the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with them.
In that regard, what is hatred as an unwholesome root?
It is malice toward sentient beings, intolerance, ill will, malevolence, the desire for harm, and mental repulsion; this is hatred as an unwholesome root.
What is its root?
It is the root of bodily action, verbal action, and mental action born of hatred, as well as of the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with them.
In this context, what is delusion as an unwholesome root?
That which is non-realization, non-comprehension, and non-penetration regarding the Four Noble Truths— delusion, being deluded, complete delusion, total bewilderment,
ignorance, darkness, blindness, obstruction, hindrance, covering, concealing,
and the failure to see clearly with respect to wholesome states— this is delusion, the unwholesome root.
What is the root of this?
It is the root of deluded unwholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, as well as of the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with them.
In this regard, the perversions should be known, and the basis for the perversions should be known.
Whatever perversion there may be, that should be known.
In this context, there is one perversion, three perversions, and four bases for perversion.
What is the one perversion, and by what opposite factor is it perverted so that one grasps it?
“To take the impermanent as permanent,” “to take suffering as happiness,” “to take what is non-self as self,” and “to take the foul as beautiful”—this is one perversion.
What are the four bases for perversion?
They are the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
These are the four bases for perversion.
What are the three perversions?
Perception, mind, and view.
These are the three perversions (*vipallāsa*).

Among them, the grasping of the sign (*nimitta*) regarding an agreeable object—whether in the sense-base of the faculties or in the sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*)—is the perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*).
Therein, the manifestation of consciousness (*viññatti*) toward an object by one whose mind is perverted is the perversion of mind (*citta-vipallāsa*).

In that regard, for one whose mind is perverted, whatever acceptance, preference, indifference, certainty, view, demonstration, and investigation there is toward that form as "beautiful in what is ugly"—this is the perversion of view (*diṭṭhivipallāsa*).
Therein, by way of the division of the bases, there are twelve perversions regarding the body:
three regarding the body, three regarding feeling, three regarding the mind, and three regarding phenomena; likewise, there are four perversions of perception and four perversions of mind.

There are four perversions of view. From the accumulation of sense bases, there are twelve perversions for one possessing eye-consciousness and perception regarding forms, and so on up to twelve perversions for one possessing mind-consciousness and perception regarding mental phenomena (*dhammas*). Thus, six sets of twelve make forty-eight perversions.
Indeed, due to the diversity of objects, there are immeasurable and incalculable perversions for immeasurable and incalculable beings, according to their inferior, superior, or middling nature.
In this context, the five aggregates constitute the four bases of personal existence (*attabhāvavatthu*).
That which is the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is the body as a base of personal existence;
that which is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is feeling as a base of personal existence.
The aggregate of perception and the aggregate of mental formations—these phenomena are the basis for the personal existence.
The aggregate of consciousness is the mind, which is the basis for the personal existence.
Thus, the five aggregates constitute the four bases for personal existence.
Therein, regarding the body, there is the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive.
Likewise regarding feelings...
There is a perversion of self regarding the mind and regarding mental phenomena.

In this regard, for the purpose of uprooting these four perversions, the Blessed One teaches and establishes the four foundations of mindfulness: for one who dwells contemplating the body in the body, [the perception arises] "beauty in the foul."
One eradicates perversion; the same should be done regarding feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena.
In this context, ignorance has the characteristic of non-penetration, like blinding darkness and gloom; its proximate cause is perversion.
Craving has the characteristic of cleaving; its proximate cause is what is lovely and pleasant.
Greed has the characteristic of deceiving oneself; its proximate cause is taking what is not given.
Here, hatred has the characteristic of quarreling; its proximate cause is the destruction of life.
Delusion has the characteristic of misapprehending the object; its proximate cause is wrong practice.
The perception of permanence has the characteristic of grasping at the non-destruction of conditioned phenomena; its proximate cause is all formations.
The perception of pleasure has the characteristic of approaching contact accompanied by taints; its proximate cause is the sense of "mine.
The perception of self has the characteristic of approaching phenomena [as a self]; its proximate cause is the sense of "I."
The perception of beauty has the characteristic of grasping at color; its proximate cause is non-restraint of the faculties.

By these nine terms thus taught, the entire side of the unwholesome is demonstrated. Furthermore, this can be understood by one who is well-learned, not by one who is ill-learned; by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted; and by one who is disciplined, not by one who is undisciplined.
These nine wholesome terms are those wherein the entire side of the wholesome is included and converges.
What are the nine factors?
Serenity, insight, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception of foulness.
In this context, what is serenity?

That which is the stability, steadfastness, firmness, state, foundation, presence, concentration, composure, non-distraction, freedom from remorse, tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind—this is serenity (*samatha*).
In this context, what is insight (*vipassanā*)?
It is [the contemplation] upon the aggregates, or the elements, or the sense-bases, or name-and-form, or dependent origination, or dependently arisen phenomena.
Or, regarding phenomena that are suffering, or origins, or cessations, or paths; or regarding phenomena that are wholesome or unwholesome,
blameworthy or blameless, dark or bright, to be cultivated or not to be cultivated— that which is the investigation,
thorough investigation, inquiry, thorough inquiry, fathoming, thorough fathoming, encompassing, thorough encompassing, mental cultivation, and weighing of these as they truly are.

Investigation, knowledge, science, vision, intelligence, wisdom, insight, illumination, light, radiance, effulgence, the sword, the thunderbolt, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, and right view as a path-factor—this is insight (*vipassanā*).
For this reason it is called "insight. Alternatively, because this insight is manifold (*vividhā*), it is therefore called "insight" (*vipassanā*).
For this insight is twofold; it is called "insight into phenomena" (*dhamma-vipassanā*). By means of this, one sees in two ways:

the beautiful and the ugly, the dark and the bright, what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, action and its result, bondage and liberation, accumulation and diminution, occurrence and cessation, defilement and purification. Thus...
It is called *vipassanā*. Alternatively, *vi* is a prefix and *passanā* means "seeing"; therefore it is called *vipassanā*. This is *vipassanā*.

In this regard, there are two diseases for sentient beings: ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). For the destruction of these two diseases, the Blessed One has prescribed two medicines: serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

By partaking of these two medicines, one realizes two states of health: the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust (*rāgavirāga-cetovimutti*) and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance (*avijjāvirāga-paññāvimutti*).
In this regard, serenity (*samatha*) is the medicine for the disease of craving; the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the state of health.
Insight (*vipassanā*) is the medicine for the disease of ignorance; the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the state of health.
For thus the Blessed One has said: "Two things are to be fully understood: name and form. Two things are to be abandoned:
ignorance and craving for existence. Two things are to be developed: serenity and insight. Two things are to be realized:
true knowledge and liberation."
Therein, by developing serenity, one fully understands form; fully understanding form, one abandons craving;
abandoning craving, one realizes the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust. By developing insight, one fully understands the mental (name);
fully understanding the mental, one abandons ignorance; abandoning ignorance, one realizes the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.
When two things have been fully understood by a bhikkhu—namely, name and form—then two things have been abandoned by him: ignorance and craving for existence.
Two things have been developed by him: serenity and insight. Two things have been realized by him: true knowledge and liberation.
To this extent, a bhikkhu has accomplished his task.
This is the element of nibbāna with residue remaining.
With the exhaustion of his lifespan and the cessation of the life-faculty, this suffering ceases and no further suffering arises.

In that regard, the cessation and subsiding of these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and the non-relinking and non-manifestation of other aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—this is the element of nibbāna without residue remaining.
In this context, what is the wholesome root of non-greed?
That which is non-greed, non-covetousness, the state of being without covetousness, lack of desire, lack of longing, lack of attraction, and lack of attachment—
this is the wholesome root of non-greed.
What is the root of this?
It is the root of wholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action born of non-greed, as well as of the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with them.
Alternatively, the Noble Eightfold Path is called "wholesome," and it is the root of three path-factors.
Of which three? Of right intention, right effort, and right concentration—of these it is the root; therefore it is called a wholesome root (*kusalamūla*).
In that regard, what is the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa*)?

That which is the absence of malice, the absence of resentment, the absence of ill-will, the absence of malevolence, non-hatred, loving-kindness (*mettā*), the state of being loving, the desire for welfare, the desire for benefit, and serenity of mind toward sentient beings or conditioned phenomena—this is the wholesome root of non-hatred.
What is its root?
It is the root of wholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action that are free from hatred, as well as of the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with them.
Alternatively, it is the root of three factors of the path.
Of which three?
Of these three path-factors: right speech, right action, and right livelihood. Therefore, it is called a root of the wholesome.
In that regard, what is the root of the wholesome that is non-delusion?
That which is the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are regarding the four noble truths— namely, realization, right re-attainment,
penetration, non-delusion, non-confusion, absence of delusion, the illumination of true knowledge, light, and non-obstruction of the wholesome states of those in training—
this is the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is its root?
It is the root of wholesome bodily action, verbal action, and mental action born of non-delusion, as well as of the states of consciousness and mental factors associated with them.
Alternatively, it is the root of two factors of the Path.
Of which two?
Of right view and right mindfulness—of these two path-factors it is the root; therefore it is called a "wholesome root.
In this way, the eightfold path is to be connected with these three wholesome roots.
In this context, what is the perception of impermanence?
The perception, the act of perceiving, the defining, and the grasping that "all conditioned phenomena are subject to arising and passing away"—this is the perception of impermanence.
What is its outflow?

When the perception of impermanence has been developed and cultivated, the mind does not flow along with, does not flow toward, and does not settle upon the eight worldly conditions; rather, either equanimity or repulsiveness settles there. This is its outflow.
In this context, what is the perception of suffering?
The perception, the act of perceiving, the defining, and the grasping that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering"—this is the perception of suffering.
What is its outcome?

When the perception of suffering has been developed and cultivated, the mind does not incline toward, does not flow toward, and does not settle upon indolence, negligence, or bewilderment; rather, either equanimity or repulsiveness settles there—this is its outcome.
In this context, what is the perception of non-self?
“The perception, the act of perceiving, the defining, the grasping that ‘all phenomena are non-self’—this is the perception of non-self (*anattasaññā*).

What is its outflow? When the perception of non-self has been developed and cultivated, the mind does not continue in or incline toward the notion of ‘I,’ nor does it settle upon the notion of ‘mine. Either equanimity or repulsiveness settles there; this is its outflow.
In this context, what is the perception of the unattractive (*asubhasaññā*)?”
“The seven formations are foul”: whatever perception, perceiving, defining, and grasping there is [regarding this], this is the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*).
What is its outflow?

When the perception of foulness has been developed and cultivated, the mind does not follow after, does not flow toward, and does not settle upon a sign of beauty; rather, either equanimity or repulsiveness settles [there]. This is its outflow.
In that regard, the full understanding of the five aggregates has been taught by the Blessed One: therein, the perception of foulness is the full understanding of the aggregate of form;

the perception of suffering is the full understanding of the aggregate of feeling; the perception of non-self is the full understanding of the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of mental formations;
and the perception of impermanence is the full understanding of the aggregate of consciousness.

Therein, by means of serenity (samatha), one eradicates craving (taṇhā); by means of insight (vipassanā), one eradicates ignorance (avijjā); by means of non-hatred (adosa), one eradicates hatred (dosa); by means of non-delusion (amoha), one eradicates delusion (moha);
by means of the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), one eradicates the perception of permanence (niccasaññā);

by means of the perception of suffering (dukkhasaññā), one eradicates the perception of pleasure (sukhasaññā); by means of the perception of non-self (anattasaññā), one eradicates the perception of self (attasaññā); by means of the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā)...
It eradicates the perception of beauty.
Tranquility has the characteristic of withdrawing the mind from distraction; its proximate cause is the jhānas.
Insight has the characteristic of penetrating all phenomena as they truly are; its proximate cause is all that is knowable.
Non-greed has the characteristic of withdrawing desire; its proximate cause is abstaining from taking what is not given.
Non-hatred has the characteristic of non-ill-will; its proximate cause is abstaining from killing living beings.
Non-delusion has the characteristic of non-obstruction toward objects; its proximate cause is right practice.
The perception of impermanence has the characteristic of grasping the destruction of conditioned phenomena; its proximate cause is arising and passing away.
The perception of suffering has the characteristic of cognizing contact accompanied by taints; its proximate cause is feeling.
The perception of non-self has the characteristic of not approaching any phenomena; its proximate cause is the perception of phenomena.
The perception of foulness has the characteristic of apprehending the livid, the festering, and the bloated; its proximate cause is disenchantment.

When these nine points have been pointed out, the entire side of the wholesome is thereby pointed out. And this can be known by one who is learned, not by one who is unlearned; by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted; and by one who is diligent, not by one who is indolent.

In that regard, for one whose mind is inclined toward the perception of permanence and who repeatedly directs the mind [toward the foul], the perception of impermanence arises when he reflects with mindfulness.

It does not arise: for one who is intent upon the gratification of pleasure in the five strands of sensual desire, the perception of suffering does not arise in one who fails to reflect on the instability of postures;

for one who is intent upon a self in the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the perception of non-self does not arise in one who fails to reflect on the analysis of various elements and manifold elements;
and for one who delights in color and shape, and is intent upon beauty in the body, [the perception of foulness] remains concealed.
The perception of foulness does not become established.
Faith has the characteristic of non-remorse; its manifestation is conviction.
Its proximate cause is the four factors of stream-entry.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of faith to be seen? It is to be seen in the four factors of stream-entry, which are wholesome states.
The faculty of energy has the characteristic of not shrinking back; its manifestation is the arousal of energy.
Its proximate cause is the four right endeavors of the past."
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of energy to be seen? In the four right strivings.
Mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering; its manifestation is non-delusion.
Its proximate cause is the four past foundations of mindfulness.
As it was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of mindfulness to be seen? In the four foundations of mindfulness.
Concentration has the characteristic of one-pointedness, and its manifestation is non-distraction; its proximate cause is the four kinds of knowledge. As it was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of concentration to be seen? In the four jhānas.”
Wisdom has the characteristic of understanding; its manifestation is the investigation of the true nature of things;
its proximate cause is the Four Noble Truths. As it was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, where is the faculty of wisdom to be seen? In the Four Noble Truths. There are four wheels:
dwelling in a suitable locality is a wheel; reliance on a person of integrity is a wheel; right self-application is a wheel; and merit performed in the past is a wheel.
In this context, dwelling in a suitable locality is characterized by reliance on the noble ones;
it is the proximate cause for relying on true persons. Relying on true persons is characterized by reliance on the noble ones;
it is the proximate cause for right aspiration toward oneself. Right aspiration toward oneself is characterized by correct practice; it is the proximate cause for meritorious deeds.
Merit has the characteristic of accumulating wholesome states; it is the proximate cause for all forms of success.

There are eleven qualities rooted in virtue: for one who possesses virtue, there is freedom from remorse … [and so on] … he attains the knowledge and vision of liberation, the realization that "there is no further state of being."
In this context, virtue has the characteristic of abstinence; it is the proximate cause for non-remorse.
Non-remorse has the characteristic of not reproaching oneself; it is the proximate cause for gladness.
Gladness has the characteristic of mental upliftment; it is the proximate cause for rapture.
Rapture has the characteristic of mental elation; it is the proximate cause for tranquility.
Tranquility has the characteristic of serviceability; it is the proximate cause for happiness.
Happiness has the characteristic of non-affliction; it is the proximate cause for concentration.
Concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction; it is the proximate cause for knowledge and vision of things as they truly are.
Wisdom has the characteristic of unerring investigation; it is the proximate cause for disenchantment. Disenchantment has the characteristic of non-attachment;
it is the proximate cause for dispassion. Dispassion has the characteristic of non-affliction; it is the proximate cause for liberation.
Liberation has the characteristic of seclusion from unwholesome states; it is the proximate cause for the purification of one who is liberated.
There are four noble planes and four fruits of recluseship.
In this regard, one who understands them as they truly are—this is the plane of vision.
Having understood the fruit of stream-entry as it really is, one becomes disenchanted; this is the proximate cause for the thinning of sensual desire and ill will.
One becomes detached from the fruit of once-returning with subtlety; this is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust.
And that which is liberated through the fading away of ignorance regarding the fruit of non-returning—this is the ground of what has been done.

And what is the meaning of the term "fruits of recluseship" (sāmaññaphala) including Arahantship? The Noble Eightfold Path is "recluseship" (sāmañña); these are its fruits, and thus they are called "fruits of recluseship.
Why are they called "fruits of brahminhood" (brahmaññaphala)?
The Noble Eightfold Path is "brahminhood" (brahmañña); these are its fruits, and thus they are called "fruits of brahminhood."
In this regard, how is one a stream-enterer?
Simultaneously with the realization of the Truths, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple:
personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances. Through the abandoning and total destruction of these three fetters, he becomes a noble disciple.
The stream-enterer is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms; he makes an end of suffering.
In this context, what is the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)?
It is when an uninstructed, foolish worldling—one who is unskilled in the noble Dharma—regards form as the self.
As far as consciousness, [if one regards] the self therein—this is the grasping at a self or the grasping at what belongs to a self among these five aggregates.
Thinking, "I am this," one is placed in control over one part, supported and dwelling upon it, moving from limb to limb.
Whatever acceptance, preference, regard, reflection on modes, contemplation of views, or conviction there is in one who has become thus—this is called the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).
Among those, five views belong to annihilationism.
Which five?
One regards form as self, up to regarding consciousness as self—these five belong to annihilationism; the remaining fifteen belong to eternalism.
Thus, with the abandoning of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), the sixty-two types of speculative views are abandoned.
With their abandonment, one does not resort to annihilationism or eternalism.
Thus, with the abandoning of annihilationism and eternalism, no speculative view remains for the noble disciple, other than the supramundane right view of full knowledge.
But how does personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) not come to be?
Here, the noble disciple is learned; the entire "white side" [of the path] should be applied, up until he is skilled in the noble qualities and regards form as non-self, up until consciousness...
[and so on]. For one who regards it in this way, personality-belief does not come to be.
How does doubt not arise?
Here, a noble disciple does not waver, does not doubt, but has full confidence in the Buddha, [thinking]: "Thus indeed is that Blessed One," and so forth for all [the epithets].
He does not waver, does not doubt in the Dhamma, and so forth for all.
He is endowed with this second quality desired by the world: "The destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
He has no doubt regarding the Saṅgha... [as before] ...up to:
"It is worthy of veneration by both gods and humans"—he is endowed with this third quality desired by the world.
He does not doubt, does not waver, is resolved, and has full confidence that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
He does not doubt, does not waver that "craving is the origin of suffering.
He does not doubt, does not waver that "with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of suffering."
He does not doubt, does not waver, is resolved, and has full confidence that "the Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.

To whatever extent there is doubting, perplexity, uncertainty, a forked path, sliding back and forth, instability, indecisiveness, or lack of single-mindedness regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, or suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path— [all these he abandons].
Uncertainty is abandoned by them, dispelled, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and subject to non-arising in the future.
In that regard, clinging to rules and observances is twofold:
Either of virtue or of purity.
Therein, regarding virtue, the adherence to rules and observances is as follows:
"By means of this virtue, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or some other kind of deity; there I shall sport with celestial nymphs with pigeon-feet."
"I shall delight; I shall serve.

"Seeing according to reality" (*yathābhūtadassana*) consists of: inclination, liberation, lust, the turning away from lust, view, conceptualization, seeing, and for one who is not content, the adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).
In this regard, what is the adherence to rules and observances of one who is pure?

In this case, someone misapprehends virtue, thinking: "One is purified by virtue, led by virtue, and liberated by virtue; one transcends pleasure, transcends pain, and transcends both pleasure and pain, attaining what lies beyond.
They misapprehend both these virtues and vows, thinking: "By means of both these virtues and vows, they are purified, liberated, and led;
they transcend pleasure, transcend pain, and transcend both pleasure and pain, attaining [the goal]."

The acceptance, preference, release, regard, reflection on modes, pondering of views, and seeing of one who returns from purity and liberation to a doctrine that does not produce purity and does not produce liberation— one who is thus constituted—
this is the adherence to rules and observances of one who is pure.

Both these misapprehensions have been abandoned by the noble disciple and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. He becomes virtuous, endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, [and so forth]—leading to peace.
Through the abandoning of these three fetters, the learned noble disciple becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, assured, and bound for full enlightenment.
All this occurs through the realization of the truths. What is the meaning of the phrase "through the realization of the truths"?
There are four kinds of clear realization: clear realization as full understanding, clear realization as abandoning, clear realization as verification, and clear realization as development.

Therein, the noble disciple clearly realizes suffering through clear realization as full understanding; he clearly realizes the origin through clear realization as abandoning; he clearly realizes cessation through clear realization as verification; and he clearly realizes the path through clear realization as development. What is the reason for this?

The clear realization through full understanding of suffering; the clear realization through abandoning of its origin; the clear realization through realizing its cessation; and the clear realization through developing the path. How does one clearly realize through serenity and insight?
Having bound the mind to the object, one sees the five aggregates as suffering.
In this context, that which is the anchoring is serenity (*samatha*);
that which is the thorough investigation is insight (*vipassanā*).

For one who sees the five aggregates as suffering, whatever attachment, inclination, approaching, cleaving, desire, infatuation, aspiration, and longing there may be toward the five aggregates is abandoned.
Therein, the five aggregates are suffering.
Whatever attachment, clinging, approaching, adherence, desire, infatuation, longing, and aspiration there is toward them—that is the origin.

Their abandonment is cessation; and serenity and insight are the path. Thus, there occurs the realization of these four noble truths at one time, at one moment, in one consciousness, neither before nor after.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “With the breakthrough to truth, three fetters are abandoned in a noble disciple.

In this context, serenity and insight, proceeding in union, perform four functions simultaneously, at one time, in one moment, within one consciousness: it breaks through suffering by means of the breakthrough of full understanding, and so on, up to breaking through the path by means of the breakthrough of development.
For what reason?
The full understanding of suffering is the realization through higher knowledge (*abhisamaya*); likewise, up to the development of the path is the realization through higher knowledge.

Thus, just as a boat traveling on the water performs four functions—it reaches the far shore, leaves the near shore, carries its cargo, and cuts through the current—so too, when serenity and insight proceed in union, at one time, at one moment, in one consciousness, they perform four functions: they realize suffering through the realization of full understanding, and so on, up to realizing the path through the realization of development.
Or just as the rising sun performs four functions simultaneously—without one being before or after the other—it dispels darkness, manifests light, makes forms visible, and terminates the cold;
even so, when serenity and insight proceed yoked together, they perform [four functions] simultaneously...
Just as a burning lamp performs four functions simultaneously—without one being before or after the other—it dispels darkness, manifests light, makes forms visible, and consumes its fuel.

In the same way, when serenity and insight proceed yoked together at the same time… [as before]… When a noble disciple becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined to make an end of suffering—this is the plane of vision.

And as for the fruit of stream-entry: established in the fruit of stream-entry and further developing serenity and insight proceeding yoked together, the noble disciple becomes one who has largely abandoned sensual lust and ill will.
Because of having reached finality as a once-returner, one returns to this world only once more and makes an end of suffering;

this is the stage of attenuation (*tanubhūmi*). And as for the fruit of once-returning: one who stands in the fruit of once-returning and develops insight abandons sensual lust and ill will together with their underlying tendencies without remainder.

When sensual lust and ill will have been abandoned without remainder, the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiyasaṃyojana*)— [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full list of the five lower fetters typically includes: 1. identity view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), 2. doubt (*vicikicchā*), 3. attachment to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), 4. sensual lust (*kāmacchanda*), and 5. ill will (*vyāpāda*).*
Sakkāyadiṭṭhi, sīlabbataparāmāsa, vicikicchā, kāmacchanda, and byāpāda are abandoned.

Through the abandoning of these five lower fetters, the noble disciple becomes a non-returner who attains final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world; this is the stage of one free from lust.

One established in the fruit of non-returning, further developing serenity and insight, abandons the five higher fetters: lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

Through the abandoning of these five higher fetters, the noble disciple becomes an arahant—one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done, who has laid down the burden, who has attained his own goal, and whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed. This is the plane of the accomplished;
this indeed is the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining.
With the exhaustion of his lifespan and the cessation of the life-faculty, this suffering ceases and no other suffering arises.
This cessation and subsiding of this suffering, and the non-manifestation of another, is the element of Nibbāna without residue.
These are the two elements of Nibbāna.

Thus the truths have been stated. The realization of the truths has been stated; the definition of the defilements has been stated; their abandonment has been stated; the stages have been stated; the fruits have been stated; and the elements of Nibbāna have been stated.
When these have thus been stated, all enlightenment is thereby stated.
In this regard, application should be practiced.
Therein, what are the nine successive attainments?
They are the four jhānas, the four formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation.
In that regard, what are the four jhānas?
Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [the rest] should be recited in detail.
In that regard, what are the four formless attainments?
One who is dispassionate should indeed be spoken to; this should be done in detail up to the attainment of cessation.
These are the nine successive attainments.
In that regard, what is the first jhāna?
It is dissociated from five factors and endowed with five factors.
From which five factors is it dissociated?
From the five hindrances.
In this context, what are the five hindrances?
"Sensual desire" is to be expanded upon.
In this context, what is sensual desire?

Whatever desire and lust, affection, attachment, cleaving, wish, infatuation, longing, non-renunciation, underlying tendency, and obsession there is toward the five strands of sensual pleasure—this is the hindrance of sensual desire.
In that regard, what is the hindrance of ill will?
Whatever malice there is toward sentient beings and conditioned phenomena... [and so on].
As with the fault, so too with its removal; this is the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
In that regard, what is torpor (*middha*)?
That which is dullness of mind, heaviness of mind, unwieldiness of mind, the casting down of mind, drowsiness, nodding, dozing, and the state of being drowsy—this is torpor.
In this context, what is sloth (*thina*)?
That which is the body’s sluggishness, its dullness, its heaviness, and its lack of tranquility—this is sloth.
Thus, this sloth together with the aforementioned torpor (*middha*) are both called the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddhanīvaraṇa*).
Therein, what is restlessness?
That which is the lack of tranquility of the mind—this is restlessness.
Therein, what is worry?
That which is a mental scarifying, brooding, worrying, heart-scarifying, and remorse—this is worry (*kukkucca*).
Thus, this worry and the aforementioned restlessness (*uddhacca*) together are called the hindrance of restlessness-and-worry (*uddhaccakukkucca-nīvaraṇa*).
In this context, what is the hindrance of doubt (*vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa*)?
Doubt regarding the Buddha, or the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha... [as before] ...this is doubt.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of doubt: that which obstructs immediate progress, that which obstructs movement to another place, that which obstructs meditative attainment, that which obstructs the Path, and that which obstructs heaven—these are the five kinds of doubt.
But here, doubt that obstructs attainment is intended.
These are the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
In this context, what is the etymological meaning of "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*), and from what do they keep one back?
They ward off everything belonging to the side of the unwholesome.
How do they ward it off?
Sensual desire is warded off by means of the foul (asubha); ill will is warded off by means of loving-kindness (mettā); sloth is warded off by means of tranquility (passaddhi).
Drowsiness prevents the arousal of energy; restlessness prevents serenity; remorse prevents non-regret;
and doubt prevents wisdom and dependent origination.
This is another method.
Sensual desire prevents one from non-greed, which is a root of the wholesome; ill will prevents one from non-hatred; sloth and torpor prevent one from concentration;
restlessness and remorse prevent one from the foundations of mindfulness; and doubt prevents one from non-delusion, which is a root of the wholesome.
Another method:
There are three abidings—the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, and the noble abiding.
The divine abiding consists of the four jhānas; the sublime abiding consists of the four immeasurables; the noble abiding consists of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment.

In this context, sensual desire, restlessness, and worry obstruct the divine abidings; ill will obstructs the sublime abidings; and sloth-torpor and doubt obstruct the noble abidings. There is another method:
sensual desire, ill will, and restlessness-and-worry obstruct calm (samatha); sloth-torpor and doubt obstruct insight (vipassanā). Therefore, they are called hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
The first jhāna is dissociated from these five factors.
From which five factors is the first jhāna associated?
It is associated with applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā).
The arising, acquisition, possession, and realization of these five factors is called "having attained the first jhāna.
Because one dwells having produced these five factors, it is said: "Having entered upon the first jhāna, he dwells" by means of a divine abiding.
Therein, the second jhāna is endowed with four factors: rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind internally.
Having aroused and fulfilled these four factors through serene confidence, he dwells; therefore it is said that "he enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
Therein, the third jhāna is endowed with five factors: mindfulness, clear comprehension, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Having aroused and accomplished these five factors through equanimity (*upekkhā*), he dwells; therefore it is said that "he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

In that context, the fourth jhāna is endowed with four factors: purity of mindfulness through equanimity, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). The fourth jhāna is thus endowed with these four factors.
Thus, the arising, the acquisition, the possession, and the realization of these four factors is called "having attained the fourth jhāna.
Having aroused and perfected these four jhānas, he enters and dwells in them; therefore, it is said that "he dwells in a divine abiding.
In this context, what is the meaning of impermanence?
The meaning of oppression is the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of disintegration, the meaning of reaching [the end], and the meaning of seclusion; this is the meaning of impermanence.
In that regard, what is the meaning of suffering?
The meaning of oppression is the meaning of suffering, the meaning of being oppressed, the meaning of agitation, and the meaning of affliction; this is the meaning of suffering.
In this context, what is the meaning of emptiness (*suññaṭṭha*)?
The meaning of being unstained, the meaning of non-association, the meaning of having gone away, the meaning of turning away—this is the meaning of emptiness.
In this context, what is the meaning of non-self (*anattaṭṭha*)?

The meaning of non-self is the meaning of being without mastery, the meaning of not being subject to one's will, the meaning of acting against one's desire, and the meaning of being thoroughly penetrated; this is the meaning of non-self.
Thus ends the *Peṭakabhūmi* from the *Saṃvattisantika*, titled "The Compendium of the Meaning of the Suttas."
